what_it_does: The semiconductor industry has standardized a new data format called MXFP4 that stores each number in just 4 bits (instead of the usual 16 or 32), which could cut AI model memory and compute costs dramatically. The problem is that language model activations contain occasional very large 'outlier' values that MXFP4 represents terribly, breaking the model's output quality. MX+ is a minimal tweak to MXFP4 that repurposes a wasted field in the outlier's encoding to store extra precision, restoring model accuracy with negligible overhead.
method_in_detail:
The idea. MXFP4 stores numbers in groups of 32, sharing one 8-bit scale factor across the group. Within each group, every number gets 4 bits: 1 sign, 2 exponent, 1 mantissa bit. The largest number in the group (the 'Block Max,' or BM) sets the shared scale, which means its own private exponent is always forced to the highest possible value — it is never actually used to store information. MX+ exploits this waste: since the BM's private exponent is fixed by definition, we can repurpose those 2 bits as extra mantissa bits, converting the BM from 1-mantissa-bit precision to 3-mantissa-bit precision — at no change to block size or other numbers.

How it works. During conversion from standard 16-bit floating-point to MXFP4+, the BM element is identified (it is already found as part of computing the shared scale) and stored with 3 mantissa bits instead of 1. An extra 8-bit field per 32-element block records which position holds the BM. All other elements are stored identically to standard MXFP4.

Integrating with GPU math hardware. NVIDIA's latest GPUs (Blackwell architecture) have hardware units (called Tensor Cores — the chip's matrix multiply engines) that natively process MXFP4. To handle the BM's extra precision without redesigning those units, MX+ splits the BM into two ordinary MXFP4 numbers (a high half and a low half), performs the main multiply operation, then runs one additional sparse multiply operation for the high half. This incurs a modest slowdown during the prompt-processing phase but is negligible during token generation (where the hardware is underutilized anyway). An alternative hardware design adds three small units (a Block Max Detector, Forward-and-Swap Units, and a Block Max Compute Unit) outside the main multiply pipeline, processing the outlier in parallel; this adds only 0.020 mm² of chip area at 28nm.

The result. MX+ reduces the accuracy gap between MXFP4 and full-precision models by a large margin — for example, improving zero-shot task accuracy for Llama-3.1-8B from roughly 40% (broken with standard MXFP4) back toward the 70-80% seen in full precision, with storage overhead of just 0.25 additional bits per element.
